PEPTIDES.name: Semaglutide
PEPTIDES.tag: Lab-made copy of the gut hormone GLP-1. Weekly shot that curbs appetite and lowers blood sugar.
PEPTIDES.what: A modified version of GLP-1, a hormone your gut releases after eating. It slows stomach emptying and signals fullness to the brain, and helps the pancreas release insulin.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Strong. In the STEP 1 trial, adults on semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly lost an average 14.9% of body weight over 68 weeks vs 2.4% on placebo.1 In the head-to-head SURMOUNT-5 trial it produced 13.7% loss vs 20.2% for tirzepatide at 72 weeks.3
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved brand products. FDA declared the semaglutide shortage resolved on Feb 21, 2025, ending the shortage-based allowance for mass compounded copies.4 An April 1, 2026 FDA statement says it won't act against a pharmacy filling four or fewer prescriptions a month of a copy, and adding B12 doesn't automatically make it "not a copy."6 FDA has proposed excluding semaglutide from the 503B bulks list5 and in Feb 2026 announced steps against mass-marketed compounded GLP-1s.7
risks: Stomach side effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation) are common.8
With compounded multi-dose vials, FDA has reports of people injecting 5–20× the intended dose; some were hospitalized (pancreatitis, gallstones, dehydration reported).9
Fraudulent or improperly shipped products have been reported.8
PEPTIDES.route: Weekly injection (oral form for diabetes also exists)
PEPTIDES.riskShort: GI side effects; dosing errors with compounded vials

PEPTIDES.name: Tirzepatide
PEPTIDES.tag: Hits two gut-hormone receptors (GIP + GLP-1). Currently the most effective approved weight-loss shot.
PEPTIDES.what: A single peptide that activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors, two hormone signals involved in appetite and blood-sugar control.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Strong. In SURMOUNT-1, the 15 mg dose produced an average 20.9% weight loss at 72 weeks vs 3.1% on placebo.2 It beat semaglutide head-to-head (20.2% vs 13.7%) in SURMOUNT-5.3
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved brand products. Tirzepatide is no longer on FDA's shortage list, and the period of enforcement discretion for compounded copies has ended.4 It's not on the 503B bulks list, and FDA has proposed keeping it off.5,6 In 2026 FDA warned Empower Pharmacy, a major compounder, over mass copying of tirzepatide/semaglutide and insanitary conditions.32 Gray-market "research" tirzepatide has drawn FDA warning letters.12,13
risks: Same family of GI side effects as semaglutide.8
Compounded/unapproved versions skip FDA review of safety, quality, and dose; FDA has adverse-event reports tied to doses above the approved label.8

PEPTIDES.name: Retatrutide
PEPTIDES.tag: Experimental triple-hormone drug with record trial weight loss. Not approved — but already sold illegally online.
PEPTIDES.what: An investigational Eli Lilly peptide that activates three receptors at once: GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon.
claims: Knee-arthritis pain and sleep apnea (in obesity)
PEPTIDES.evidence: Promising Phase 3 results, not yet FDA-reviewed. Lilly reported average 28.3% weight loss at 80 weeks on the 12 mg dose in TRIUMPH-1.34 In TRIUMPH-2 (people with obesity and type 2 diabetes), weight loss reached 20.8% at 80 weeks with A1C reductions of up to 1.6 points.10,11 In two Phase 3 sleep-apnea trials published in NEJM in October 2026, retatrutide 9 mg and 12 mg cut breathing interruptions (apnea-hypopnea index) by 24.4 and 21.9 more events per hour than placebo at 80 weeks in adults with obesity without diabetes, and by 14.4 and 15.1 more in adults with type 2 diabetes; the most common side effects were gastrointestinal.225
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Lilly plans to submit for US approval in Q1 2027.10 FDA has sent 2026 warning letters to websites selling "research use only" retatrutide, calling it an unapproved new drug.12,13,14
risks: Full safety profile hasn't been reviewed by FDA yet.
Gray-market vials have no verified identity, purity, or dose.12

PEPTIDES.name: BPC-157
PEPTIDES.tag: The poster child of biohacking peptides, hyped for healing tendons and guts. Human data is almost nonexistent.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide based on a protein found in stomach juice.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mostly rats and lab dishes. A 2025 systematic review found 36 studies: 35 preclinical and 1 small human study (7 of 12 knee-pain patients reported relief), and no human safety data.15 A second review counted only three small human pilot studies and no large trials.16
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. FDA moved it off its Category 2 "significant safety concerns" compounding list on Apr 22, 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn — which did not add it to the list of substances pharmacies may compound.17,31 On July 23, 2026 FDA's advisory committee voted 8–6 (1 abstention) to recommend adding it, against FDA staff's advice; the vote is advisory.18 As of Oct 9, 2026, FDA hadn't proposed a rule or moved it to Category 1.19 On Oct 7, 2026 the Washington Post reported the administration is preparing a temporary stopgap (enforcement discretion) that could let licensed compounding pharmacies sell some of the July-recommended peptides while permanent rules are written; it hadn't been announced or taken effect, and FDA drug-center staff reportedly said they won't recommend it.183,184 On Oct 14, 2026 FDA sent an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" to the White House regulatory office (OIRA) for review; it isn't published or in effect, and it doesn't name the peptides.187 OIRA has logged outside meetings on it for Oct 21, 23 and 27, and HHS Secretary Kennedy said on Oct 20 the goal is a regulated marketplace; the text still isn't public.189,190 Banned in sport by WADA.21
risks: No controlled human safety data.15
FDA reviewers flagged basic questions about what "BPC-157" products actually contain (identity and characterization).18
Gray-market products are unregulated.
PEPTIDES.regShort: Not approved; compounding status in limbo

PEPTIDES.name: TB-500
PEPTIDES.tag: Often 'stacked' with BPC-157 for recovery. No human trials of the fragment itself.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic short fragment (Ac-LKKTETQ) of thymosin beta-4, a natural protein involved in cell movement and repair. Originally marketed for racehorses.
PEPTIDES.evidence: A 2026 scoping review found no human studies giving TB-4 or TB-500 for tendon, ligament, muscle, bone or cartilage repair; human evidence is mostly for the full-length protein in eye and skin uses.20
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Removed from FDA's Category 2 list in April 2026, not added to the compounding list.17 Advisory committee voted 8–6–1 in favor of listing in July 2026; no final FDA action as of Oct 9, 2026; a temporary enforcement-discretion stopgap was reported under consideration on Oct 7 (not announced or in effect).18,19,183 On Oct 14, 2026 FDA sent an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" to the White House regulatory office (OIRA) for review; it isn't published or in effect, and it doesn't name the peptides.187 OIRA has logged outside meetings on it for Oct 21, 23 and 27, and HHS Secretary Kennedy said on Oct 20 the goal is a regulated marketplace; the text still isn't public.189,190 Prohibited at all times by WADA.21
risks: FDA has cited limited human exposure and safety data.20
Results from the full-length protein can't be assumed to apply to the fragment.
PEPTIDES.regShort: Not approved; compounding status in limbo

PEPTIDES.name: GHK-Cu
PEPTIDES.tag: A copper-binding tripeptide found in skincare serums — and increasingly injected. Lab data looks good; human data is thin.
PEPTIDES.what: A tiny three-amino-acid peptide (glycine-histidine-lysine) bound to copper, naturally present in blood plasma.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Extensive cell and animal research on collagen production and wound repair; human studies are mostly small cosmetic trials, many industry-linked.22 No large, independent trials of injected GHK-Cu.
PEPTIDES.reg: Topical creams are sold as cosmetics. Injectable GHK-Cu was removed from FDA's Category 2 list in April 2026 and is slated for an FDA advisory committee review before the end of Feb 2027.17,31
risks: Injected use hasn't been tested in controlled trials.
Gray-market injectables have unverified purity.
PEPTIDES.regShort: Cosmetic topically; injectable under FDA review

PEPTIDES.name: CJC-1295 + Ipamorelin
PEPTIDES.tag: Popular clinic 'stack' to boost natural growth hormone for muscle, fat loss and sleep. Wellness claims are untested.
PEPTIDES.what: CJC-1295 mimics GHRH (the brain signal that releases growth hormone); ipamorelin mimics ghrelin to trigger growth-hormone pulses. Together they're sold to raise GH and IGF-1.
PEPTIDES.evidence: No trials of the combination for wellness. A small 2006 study showed CJC-1295 raised GH 2–10× and IGF-1 1.5–3× in healthy adults — hormone levels, not health outcomes.23 Ipamorelin failed to show a significant benefit in a 117-patient trial for post-surgery bowel recovery.24
PEPTIDES.reg: Neither is FDA-approved, and neither is on the list of substances pharmacies may compound. FDA has flagged both in its compounding safety-risk list, citing concerns such as immunogenicity and impurities.33 Both are banned in sport by WADA.21
risks: Long-term effects of pushing GH/IGF-1 up in healthy people are unstudied.
Compounded or gray-market product quality is unverified.33
PEPTIDES.regShort: Not approved; flagged by FDA for compounding risks

PEPTIDES.name: Collagen peptides
PEPTIDES.tag: The everyday peptide in coffee and smoothies. Many trials, modest results — and independent studies are less impressed.
PEPTIDES.what: Collagen protein (usually from cows or fish) broken down into small peptides so it dissolves easily. Taken by mouth as powder or capsules.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mixed. A 2026 meta-analysis of 35 trials (2,534 people) found modest gains in skin hydration, elasticity (after ~12 weeks) and barrier function, but wrinkle and skin-density benefits looked like statistical artifacts.25 A 2025 meta-analysis found no effect in high-quality or non-industry-funded trials.26
PEPTIDES.reg: Sold as a dietary supplement. FDA doesn't approve supplements for safety or effectiveness before they're marketed.27
risks: Main risk is paying for benefits that may be small.
Supplement quality and label accuracy aren't pre-checked by FDA.27

PEPTIDES.name: SS-31 (Elamipretide)
PEPTIDES.tag: Approved for one rare disease — and now marketed online for 'mitochondrial energy' and longevity.
PEPTIDES.what: A small peptide that binds cardiolipin inside mitochondria (the cell's power plants) to support their structure and function.
PEPTIDES.evidence: FDA granted accelerated approval on Sept 19, 2025 to treat Barth syndrome, a rare mitochondrial disease, based on improved knee-muscle strength; a confirmatory trial is required.28 There's no evidence for "wellness" use in healthy people.
PEPTIDES.reg: Approved only as Forzinity for Barth syndrome.28 FDA's Aug 24, 2026 warning letters named sellers of "research" SS-31 as distributing an unapproved drug.13,14
risks: Approval rests on a tiny rare-disease population; benefits for healthy people are unknown.
Gray-market vials skip FDA quality controls.13

PEPTIDES.name: PT-141 (Bremelanotide)
PEPTIDES.tag: Approved for low sexual desire in premenopausal women; widely sold gray-market as a libido booster for anyone.
PEPTIDES.what: A peptide that activates melanocortin receptors in the brain involved in sexual desire. Used as needed, not daily.
claims: Low sexual desire (approved for one group)
Libido for men and women (off-label/gray market)
PEPTIDES.evidence: FDA approved Vyleesi in June 2019 for acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women.30 Other uses aren't approved.
PEPTIDES.reg: Approved as Vyleesi for one narrow use.30 FDA's Aug 2026 warning letters targeted websites selling "research" PT-141.13,14
risks: Nausea is common (about 40% in trials).29
Temporary rise in blood pressure; not for people with uncontrolled high blood pressure or known heart disease.29
Dark skin patches (face, gums, breasts) can occur and may not fade.29

PEPTIDES.name: Liraglutide
PEPTIDES.tag: An older daily GLP-1 shot. Less weight loss than semaglutide, but now available as generics.
PEPTIDES.what: A lab-made GLP-1 analogue, the same gut-hormone signal that semaglutide copies, taken as a daily injection.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Strong. In the 56-week SCALE trial (3,731 adults without diabetes), 63.2% on liraglutide 3.0 mg lost at least 5% of body weight vs 27.1% on placebo; the average difference was about 5.6 kg.35
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved as Victoza (type 2 diabetes, 2010)36 and Saxenda (chronic weight management, 2014).37,38 FDA has also approved generic liraglutide, starting with Hikma's in December 2024.39
risks: Boxed warning: thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents; not for people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2.38
Label warnings include pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, low blood sugar with other diabetes drugs, faster heart rate, and kidney injury from dehydration.38
Most common side effects: nausea, diarrhea, constipation, vomiting.38
PEPTIDES.riskShort: GI side effects; thyroid tumor boxed warning

PEPTIDES.name: Exenatide
PEPTIDES.tag: The first GLP-1 drug. Approved for type 2 diabetes, not for weight loss.
PEPTIDES.what: A GLP-1 receptor agonist injected to help control blood sugar in type 2 diabetes.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Approved on the basis of glycemic trials in type 2 diabetes.40 It is not FDA-approved for weight management.40
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes. The weekly versions (Bydureon, Bydureon BCise) are listed as discontinued in Drugs@FDA.41 A generic twice-daily exenatide (Amneal) is approved.42
risks: Label warnings include pancreatitis, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, kidney injury from dehydration, and severe GI reactions; not recommended with severe gastroparesis.40
PEPTIDES.riskShort: GI effects; pancreatitis; low blood sugar with insulin

PEPTIDES.name: Pramlintide
PEPTIDES.tag: Lab-made version of amylin, the hormone the newer 'amylin' weight-loss drugs are built on.
PEPTIDES.what: An analogue of amylin, a hormone made alongside insulin that slows stomach emptying and lowers after-meal glucose. Used with mealtime insulin.
claims: After-meal blood sugar in type 1 and type 2 diabetes
PEPTIDES.evidence: Approved as an add-on to mealtime insulin in type 1 and type 2 diabetes.43 It is not approved for weight loss.43
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (Symlin, 2005), but Drugs@FDA now lists Symlin's marketing status as discontinued.44
risks: Boxed warning: severe low blood sugar when used with insulin, especially in type 1 diabetes.43
Common side effects: nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, headache.43

PEPTIDES.name: Setmelanotide
PEPTIDES.tag: Approved for rare genetic and brain-injury forms of obesity, not everyday weight loss.
PEPTIDES.what: A melanocortin-4 (MC4) receptor agonist that restores a brain appetite pathway broken in certain rare genetic conditions.
claims: Weight loss in rare genetic obesity
PEPTIDES.evidence: In a phase 3 trial in Bardet-Biedl syndrome, 32.3% of patients aged 12+ lost at least 10% of body weight after 52 weeks.45 It's approved only for specific diagnoses.46
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (2020)47 for obesity due to Bardet-Biedl syndrome or genetically confirmed POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency (age 2+), and acquired hypothalamic obesity (age 4+). Not for general obesity.46
risks: Skin darkening (hyperpigmentation) and darkening of moles are common.46,45
Label warnings include depression and suicidal thoughts, and sexual arousal effects (spontaneous erections).46
Other common effects: injection-site reactions, nausea, headache.46

PEPTIDES.name: Survodutide
PEPTIDES.tag: Glucagon + GLP-1 dual agonist with positive phase 3 weight-loss results. Not approved.
PEPTIDES.what: An injectable peptide that activates both glucagon and GLP-1 receptors, aiming to reduce appetite and increase energy use.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3 data. In SYNCHRONIZE-1, weight fell 12.2% (3.6 mg) and 13.0% (6.0 mg) at 76 weeks vs 5.4% on placebo.48 In SYNCHRONIZE-2 (755 adults with obesity/overweight and type 2 diabetes, NEJM, Oct 5, 2026), weight fell up to 13.1% at 76 weeks vs 3.1% on placebo, with HbA1c down up to 1.21 points (efficacy estimand).185
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational, not FDA-approved. Products sold online as 'research' survodutide are not the trial drug.
risks: GI side effects (mostly mild to moderate) occurred in 81–90% of participants on survodutide vs 48% on placebo.48
In SYNCHRONIZE-2, 18% stopped survodutide because of GI side effects vs 1.2% on placebo.185
Long-term safety still under study.

PEPTIDES.name: Mazdutide
PEPTIDES.tag: GLP-1 + glucagon dual agonist tested in large Chinese trials. Not approved in the US.
PEPTIDES.what: A once-weekly injectable peptide that activates GLP-1 and glucagon receptors.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3 data. In GLORY-1 (610 Chinese adults), weight fell 11.0% (4 mg) and 14.0% (6 mg) at 48 weeks vs a 0.3% gain on placebo.49
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved; no US approval found.
risks: GI side effects, mostly mild to moderate, were the most common adverse events.49
Studied mainly in Chinese adults; US data limited.49

PEPTIDES.name: Cagrilintide
PEPTIDES.tag: Long-acting amylin analogue. The 'Cagri' half of CagriSema.
PEPTIDES.what: A long-acting analogue of the hormone amylin, which signals fullness and slows stomach emptying.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 2: over 26 weeks, weight fell 6.0–10.8% across doses vs 3.0% on placebo; the top dose beat liraglutide 3 mg (10.8% vs 9.0%).50
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational alone; not FDA-approved.
risks: GI side effects (nausea, constipation, diarrhea) affected 41–63% on cagrilintide vs 32% on placebo.50

PEPTIDES.name: CagriSema
PEPTIDES.tag: Weekly combo of an amylin analogue with semaglutide. Big phase 3 results; not approved yet.
PEPTIDES.what: A fixed combination of cagrilintide (amylin analogue) and semaglutide (GLP-1) given together.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3. In REDEFINE 1, average weight fell 20.4% at 68 weeks vs 3.0% on placebo.51
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved as of this update.
risks: GI adverse events in about 80% of participants on CagriSema.51

PEPTIDES.name: Amycretin
PEPTIDES.tag: One molecule that hits both GLP-1 and amylin receptors. Early but striking results.
PEPTIDES.what: A single peptide engineered to activate both GLP-1 and amylin receptors.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Early-phase. In a phase 1b/2a trial, the highest dose (60 mg) produced up to 24.3% weight loss at 36 weeks.52 Trials were small and short.
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: GI side effects were the most common, mostly mild to moderate; many participants withdrew, often for reasons unrelated to side effects.52
PEPTIDES.riskShort: GI side effects; early data only

PEPTIDES.name: Eloralintide
PEPTIDES.tag: Lilly's selective amylin receptor agonist. Strong phase 2; phase 3 under way.
PEPTIDES.what: A selective amylin receptor agonist given as a weekly injection.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 2: up to about 20% average weight loss at 48 weeks.53 A phase 3 program has started.54
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: Nausea and fatigue were the most common side effects (nausea in up to 64% at some doses vs 14% on placebo).53

PEPTIDES.name: Petrelintide
PEPTIDES.tag: Long-acting amylin analogue partnered with Roche. Phase 3 now planned.
PEPTIDES.what: A long-acting amylin analogue designed for once-weekly dosing.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Early-phase. In phase 1 trials, weight fell up to 8.6% over 16 weeks; half-life was about 10 days.55 A Roche phase 3 trial is registered.56
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: GI side effects such as nausea were the main adverse events in phase 1.55

PEPTIDES.name: Pemvidutide
PEPTIDES.tag: GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist being developed mainly for fatty liver disease.
PEPTIDES.what: A GLP-1/glucagon dual receptor agonist peptide.
PEPTIDES.evidence: In a 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled study in MASLD, liver fat fell 47–69% (relative) and body weight also dropped vs placebo.57
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: No severe or serious adverse events in the 12-week study; longer-term safety is still being studied.57

PEPTIDES.name: Cotadutide
PEPTIDES.tag: A GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist that reached phase 2b.
PEPTIDES.what: A GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist peptide studied in type 2 diabetes and fatty liver.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 2b (54 weeks): lowered HbA1c and body weight vs placebo, but nausea (35%) and vomiting (17%) were common.58
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; never FDA-approved.
risks: High rates of nausea and vomiting.58

PEPTIDES.name: Ecnoglutide
PEPTIDES.tag: A 'biased' GLP-1 agonist with phase 3 results from China.
PEPTIDES.what: A GLP-1 receptor agonist engineered to favor one signaling pathway (cAMP-biased).
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3 in Chinese adults: 9.1–13.2% weight loss at 40 weeks vs a 0.1% gain on placebo.59
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Mild-to-moderate GI side effects were most common.59

PEPTIDES.name: VK2735
PEPTIDES.tag: A GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist (like tirzepatide). Now in phase 3.
PEPTIDES.what: An injectable dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 2 (VENTURE): 9.1–14.7% weight loss at 13 weeks vs 1.7% on placebo.60 Phase 3 is under way.61
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: GI side effects were most common, easing after dose titration; the trial lasted only 13 weeks.60
PEPTIDES.riskShort: GI side effects; short trials so far

PEPTIDES.name: CT-388
PEPTIDES.tag: Roche's GLP-1/GIP dual agonist, now in phase 3 as enicepatide.
PEPTIDES.what: A once-weekly, signaling-biased dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Early clinical data: 4.7–8.0% weight loss by day 29 in people with obesity.62 Roche is running phase 3 trials.63
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: Side effects were mostly mild or moderate, consistent with other incretin drugs; data are early.62

PEPTIDES.name: Taspoglutide
PEPTIDES.tag: An early weekly GLP-1 drug dropped after side-effect problems. A cautionary tale.
PEPTIDES.what: A weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist that was tested in phase 3 for type 2 diabetes.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3 (T-emerge 2) found unacceptable rates of nausea and vomiting plus injection-site and systemic allergic reactions; anti-drug antibodies developed in 49% of patients.64
PEPTIDES.reg: Never FDA-approved; the phase 3 report judged its nausea, injection-site and allergic reactions unacceptable.64
risks: Allergic reactions, injection-site reactions and heavy GI side effects.64

PEPTIDES.name: MET-097i
PEPTIDES.tag: An ultra-long-acting GLP-1 agonist now in Pfizer phase 3 trials.
PEPTIDES.what: A 'fully-biased', ultra long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist injection.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Completed a 28-week phase 2b (VESPER-1)65; phase 3 trials are under way.66 Peer-reviewed results were not found yet.
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: Safety profile still being established in trials.66

PEPTIDES.name: GUBamy
PEPTIDES.tag: A long-acting amylin analogue from Gubra, now owned by AbbVie. Early stage.
PEPTIDES.what: A long-acting amylin analogue in development for weight management.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Only early data. A first-in-human phase 1 study is complete67 and a phase 2 dose-finding trial is recruiting.68 No peer-reviewed results found.
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: Safety not established; full results not yet published.68

PEPTIDES.name: Ribupatide
PEPTIDES.tag: A GLP-1/GIP dual agonist from China now in phase 3, including vs semaglutide.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist peptide.
PEPTIDES.evidence: First-in-human study (90 healthy Chinese adults): after four weekly doses, weight fell 6.7–9.6% vs 1.4% on placebo.69 Phase 3 trials are under way.70
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: Mild-to-moderate side effects in early study; long-term safety unknown.69

PEPTIDES.name: Zovaglutide
PEPTIDES.tag: An experimental once-a-month GLP-1 agonist in phase 3.
PEPTIDES.what: A long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist designed for dosing every two to four weeks.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 2 (company-reported, 303 Chinese adults): 10.6–14.4% weight loss at 24 weeks vs 2.4% on placebo.71 A phase 3 trial is ongoing.72
PEPTIDES.reg: Investigational; not FDA-approved.
risks: Full peer-reviewed safety data not yet available.71

PEPTIDES.name: AOD-9604
PEPTIDES.tag: A growth-hormone fragment sold as a fat burner. Human safety data are thin.
PEPTIDES.what: A modified fragment of human growth hormone (amino acids 176-191) studied for fat breakdown.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mostly animal data, e.g., rat studies on fat metabolism.73 A 2026 sports-medicine review found rigorous human safety and efficacy data scarce.74
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. FDA's compounding safety page says it has no or limited safety information and notes serious adverse events that may be associated, though causality wasn't clear; the nomination was withdrawn.33 WADA bans AOD-9604 and hGH 176-191.21
risks: FDA lists possible serious adverse events and limited safety data.33
Gray-market purity and dose are unverified.
PEPTIDES.regShort: Not approved; withdrawn from compounding review

PEPTIDES.name: MOTS-c
PEPTIDES.tag: A peptide made by mitochondria that improved metabolism in mice. No solid human data.
PEPTIDES.what: A short peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA that acts on metabolism, studied as an 'exercise mimetic'.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mouse studies showed reduced obesity and insulin resistance.75 FDA says it has no human exposure data.33
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Removed from FDA's Category 2 list in April 2026 after a withdrawn nomination17; an advisory committee voted 7–5–2 in July 2026 to recommend it for the 503A bulks list, but FDA hadn't acted as of Oct 9, 2026; a temporary enforcement-discretion stopgap was reported under consideration on Oct 7 (not announced or in effect).18,19,183 On Oct 14, 2026 FDA sent an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" to the White House regulatory office (OIRA) for review; it isn't published or in effect, and it doesn't name the peptides.187 OIRA has logged outside meetings on it for Oct 21, 23 and 27, and HHS Secretary Kennedy said on Oct 20 the goal is a regulated marketplace; the text still isn't public.189,190 WADA bans MOTS-c (AMPK activators).21
risks: No human safety data.33
Banned in sport.21

PEPTIDES.name: Adipotide
PEPTIDES.tag: Kills the blood supply to fat in monkeys. Caused kidney changes; never made it to market.
PEPTIDES.what: A peptidomimetic designed to target and destroy blood vessels feeding white fat tissue.
PEPTIDES.evidence: In obese monkeys it caused weight loss and better insulin sensitivity, but also reversible kidney tubule changes.76 No published human trial results found.
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved; no human approval anywhere found.
risks: Kidney toxicity seen in primates.76
No human safety data.

PEPTIDES.name: KPV
PEPTIDES.tag: A three-amino-acid anti-inflammatory fragment. Promising in mouse colitis; no human trials.
PEPTIDES.what: A three-amino-acid peptide (lysine-proline-valine) studied for calming inflammation, mainly in the gut.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mouse studies: oral KPV reduced chemically induced colitis.77 FDA says it has no human exposure data.33
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Removed from FDA's Category 2 list in April 202617; an advisory committee voted 8–6–1 in July 2026 to recommend it for the 503A bulks list, but FDA hadn't acted as of Oct 9, 2026; a temporary enforcement-discretion stopgap was reported under consideration on Oct 7 (not announced or in effect).18,19,183 On Oct 14, 2026 FDA sent an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" to the White House regulatory office (OIRA) for review; it isn't published or in effect, and it doesn't name the peptides.187 OIRA has logged outside meetings on it for Oct 21, 23 and 27, and HHS Secretary Kennedy said on Oct 20 the goal is a regulated marketplace; the text still isn't public.189,190
risks: No human safety data.33
Gray-market purity and dose are unverified.

PEPTIDES.name: LL-37
PEPTIDES.tag: A natural antimicrobial peptide tested on leg ulcers. Mixed results; FDA flags safety signals.
PEPTIDES.what: A human antimicrobial peptide of the immune system, tested as a topical treatment for hard-to-heal leg ulcers.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mixed. A 2014 trial of topical LL-37 on venous leg ulcers found better healing at the two lower doses but not the highest dose78; a larger 2021 multicentre trial found no significant overall difference vs placebo.79
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Removed from Category 2 in April 2026; slated for an FDA advisory committee review by early 2027.17 FDA's safety page cites nonclinical signals of male reproductive harm and tumor-promoting effects.33
risks: FDA notes nonclinical signals of male reproductive toxicity and protumorigenic effects.33
Injected use has not been studied in trials; topical trials looked only at wounds.78,79

PEPTIDES.name: MGF
PEPTIDES.tag: An IGF-1 splice variant sold for muscle and tendon repair. Animal data only.
PEPTIDES.what: A variant of IGF-1 produced in muscle after load or injury; research mostly uses short synthetic 'MGF E-peptides'. PEG-MGF is a longer-lasting pegylated form.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Animal data, e.g., an MGF E-peptide improved healing of injured rat tendons.80 FDA says it has no human exposure data for PEG-MGF.33
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. PEG-MGF was removed from Category 2 in April 2026 and is slated for an FDA advisory committee review by early 2027.17 WADA bans mechano growth factors.21
risks: No human safety data.33
Banned in sport.21

PEPTIDES.name: Tesamorelin
PEPTIDES.tag: An approved GHRH analogue for HIV-related belly fat, often marketed off-label for 'anti-aging'.
PEPTIDES.what: A growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) analogue that prompts the pituitary to release more growth hormone.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Strong for its approved use. In a 26-week NEJM trial in HIV patients, it reduced visceral fat and raised IGF-1 by 81% vs placebo.81 Off-label anti-aging use is untested.74
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (Egrifta, 2010)82 to reduce excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV and lipodystrophy; the label says it is not indicated for weight loss.83 In 2026 FDA warned a gray-market seller of 'research' tesamorelin.13 WADA bans GHRH analogues including tesamorelin.21
risks: Label warnings: raised IGF-1, glucose intolerance or diabetes, fluid retention, and possible growth of existing tumors.83
Common side effects: joint pain, injection-site redness, swelling (edema), muscle pain.83

PEPTIDES.name: Sermorelin
PEPTIDES.tag: A once-approved GHRH fragment now sold through compounders for 'anti-aging'.
PEPTIDES.what: An analogue of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) that stimulates the pituitary to release growth hormone.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Used to test for and treat growth hormone deficiency in children: it produced catch-up growth in most, though less than daily growth hormone (somatropin).84 Adult wellness use lacks rigorous evidence.74
PEPTIDES.reg: Previously FDA-approved as Geref; Drugs@FDA lists it as discontinued.85 WADA bans sermorelin (GHRH analogues).21
risks: Facial flushing and injection-site pain were the most common side effects in pediatric use.84
Adult 'anti-aging' safety data are limited.74
Banned in sport.21

PEPTIDES.name: Hexarelin
PEPTIDES.tag: A potent growth-hormone-releasing peptide sold for muscle and recovery. Little rigorous human data.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic growth-hormone-releasing peptide (GHRP), one of the growth hormone secretagogues.
PEPTIDES.evidence: A review of growth hormone secretagogues found few long-term, rigorously controlled studies, some concern about rising blood sugar, and unknown long-term safety.86
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. WADA bans hexarelin by name.21
risks: Possible rises in blood sugar; long-term safety unknown.86
Banned in sport.21

PEPTIDES.name: GHRP-6
PEPTIDES.tag: An older growth-hormone releaser known for strong hunger. FDA keeps it on its safety-concern list.
PEPTIDES.what: An older synthetic growth-hormone-releasing peptide (GHRP) that stimulates growth hormone release.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Few rigorous human studies; long-term safety unknown.86
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Still on FDA's Category 2 list (substances with significant safety risks), citing immunogenicity, effects on cortisol and higher blood glucose.33 WADA bans GHRP-6.21
risks: FDA flags immunogenicity, cortisol effects and higher blood sugar.33
Banned in sport.21

PEPTIDES.name: Afamelanotide
PEPTIDES.tag: An approved tanning-hormone implant for a rare light-sensitivity disease. Not a cosmetic tan.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic analogue of alpha-MSH that boosts melanin in the skin. Given as an implant under the skin.
PEPTIDES.evidence: In NEJM-reported trials, EPP patients on afamelanotide had longer pain-free sun exposure (median 6.0 vs 0.8 hours in the US trial) and better quality of life.87
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (2019)88 only for adults with EPP, as an implant inserted every 2 months.89 Unregulated 'melanotan I' sold online for tanning is not this quality-controlled product.90
risks: Common side effects: implant-site reactions, nausea, skin darkening, new or darkening moles.89
Label recommends a full-body skin exam twice a year.89
PEPTIDES.route: Implant under the skin every 2 months

PEPTIDES.name: Melanotan II
PEPTIDES.tag: Unapproved 'tanning injection'. Case reports of melanoma, priapism and kidney injury.
PEPTIDES.what: An untested synthetic alpha-MSH analogue sold online, mainly to darken skin.
PEPTIDES.evidence: No controlled trials for cosmetic tanning. A review of unregulated melanotan use describes mole changes and melanoma case reports90; other case reports describe melanoma91 and priapism92.
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Removed from Category 2 in April 2026 and slated for an FDA advisory review by early 2027.17 FDA's safety page cites case reports of melanoma, PRES (a brain-swelling syndrome), sympathomimetic toxicity and priapism.33
risks: Case reports: melanoma, PRES, sympathomimetic toxidrome, priapism.33,91,92
Gray-market purity and dose are unverified.

PEPTIDES.name: Argireline
PEPTIDES.aka: Acetyl hexapeptide-3/-8; SNAP-8 is a longer analog
PEPTIDES.tag: The 'topical Botox' peptide in wrinkle creams. Small studies; poor skin penetration.
PEPTIDES.what: A short synthetic peptide used in cosmetics, claimed to relax the muscle contractions behind expression lines.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Small studies only. In a 21-person, three-arm trial on crow's feet, some users improved, but palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 did better.93 A 2025 review notes low skin penetration limits its effect.94
PEPTIDES.reg: Sold as a cosmetic ingredient. FDA does not approve cosmetics before sale (except color additives).95
risks: Main concern is overstated marketing; low skin penetration limits any effect.94

PEPTIDES.name: Matrixyl
PEPTIDES.tag: A common anti-wrinkle cream peptide. Tiny trials, modest results.
PEPTIDES.what: A fatty-acid-linked five-amino-acid peptide used in skincare to support collagen.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Small. In a 21-person randomized trial on crow's feet, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 cream did better than argireline and placebo; authors called for larger studies.93
PEPTIDES.reg: Sold as a cosmetic ingredient; FDA does not approve cosmetics before sale.95
risks: Topical; main concern is limited evidence behind marketing claims.93

PEPTIDES.name: OS-01
PEPTIDES.tag: A 'senolytic' skincare peptide. Evidence comes from company-run studies.
PEPTIDES.what: A peptide marketed as reducing senescent ('zombie') skin cells in topical products.
PEPTIDES.evidence: A double-blind, vehicle-controlled study reported improved skin texture and wrinkles with the OS-01 formula; the work was company-sponsored.96
PEPTIDES.reg: Sold in cosmetics; FDA does not approve cosmetics before sale.95
risks: Topical; independent replication is lacking.96

PEPTIDES.name: Semax
PEPTIDES.tag: A Russian nasal-spray peptide sold as a nootropic. Evidence is mostly animal and small Russian studies.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic peptide studied in Russia for stroke and marketed online for focus and memory.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mostly animal research plus small Russian clinical studies, e.g., a stroke study linking semax to higher BDNF and faster functional recovery.97 No large, independent Western trials. FDA describes its safety information as limited.33
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Removed from Category 2 in April 202617; an advisory committee voted 8–5–1 in July 2026 to recommend it for the 503A bulks list, but FDA hadn't acted as of Oct 9, 2026; a temporary enforcement-discretion stopgap was reported under consideration on Oct 7 (not announced or in effect).18,19,183 On Oct 14, 2026 FDA sent an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" to the White House regulatory office (OIRA) for review; it isn't published or in effect, and it doesn't name the peptides.187 OIRA has logged outside meetings on it for Oct 21, 23 and 27, and HHS Secretary Kennedy said on Oct 20 the goal is a regulated marketplace; the text still isn't public.189,190
risks: Limited safety information, per FDA.33
Quality of gray-market sprays is unverified.

PEPTIDES.name: Selank
PEPTIDES.tag: A Russian anti-anxiety nasal peptide. Thin evidence outside small Russian studies.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic peptide studied in Russia for anxiety.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mostly animal data plus small Russian studies, e.g., selank added to the tranquilizer phenazepam reduced its side effects in anxiety disorders.98 FDA says it lacks safety information.33
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. FDA's safety page lists it among nominated substances lacking safety information.33
risks: Safety information lacking, per FDA.33

PEPTIDES.name: Dihexa
PEPTIDES.tag: A 'brain growth' nootropic based on angiotensin IV. Rodent data only.
PEPTIDES.what: A small peptide derived from angiotensin IV that works through the HGF/c-Met growth-factor system.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Rodent studies only: dihexa improved learning in rats via the HGF/c-Met system.99 FDA says there are no human exposure data.33
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Removed from Category 2 in April 2026 and slated for an FDA advisory review by early 2027.17
risks: No human exposure data, per FDA.33

PEPTIDES.name: DSIP
PEPTIDES.tag: Sold as a sleep peptide. A controlled human trial found no meaningful benefit.
PEPTIDES.what: A small peptide named for a supposed sleep-inducing effect, sold online as a sleep aid.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Weak. In a 1992 double-blind trial in 16 people with chronic insomnia, effects were weak and the authors concluded DSIP was not likely to be of major therapeutic benefit.100 FDA says it has no safety information.33
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Removed from Category 2 in April 202617; in July 2026 it was the one peptide the FDA advisory committee did not recommend for the 503A list (vote 6–7–1).18,19
risks: No safety information, per FDA.33
PEPTIDES.riskShort: No proven benefit; no safety data

PEPTIDES.name: PE-22-28
PEPTIDES.tag: A fast-acting 'antidepressant' peptide in mice. No human studies.
PEPTIDES.what: A shortened version of spadin, a peptide that inhibits the TREK-1 channel, studied as an antidepressant in mice.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mouse studies only: PE-22-28 showed antidepressant-like effects and boosted neurogenesis.101 No published human trials found.
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No human safety data.101

PEPTIDES.name: Humanin
PEPTIDES.tag: A mitochondrial peptide studied in Alzheimer's models. No human treatment trials.
PEPTIDES.what: A small peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA that protects nerve cells against Alzheimer's-related damage in lab studies.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Cell and animal research; a 2022 review describes anti-cell-death effects in Alzheimer's models but no human treatment trials.102
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No human safety data from treatment studies.102

PEPTIDES.name: Davunetide
PEPTIDES.tag: A nerve-protecting peptide that failed its key trial.
PEPTIDES.what: A peptide that stabilized nerve-cell microtubules and reduced tau changes in preclinical studies; given as a nasal spray in trials.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Negative. A phase 2/3 trial in progressive supranuclear palsy concluded it is not an effective treatment.103
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Nasal side effects (nosebleeds, runny nose, discomfort) were more common than with placebo.103

PEPTIDES.name: Rapastinel
PEPTIDES.tag: A fast-acting depression drug candidate whose phase 3 program stalled.
PEPTIDES.what: A peptide that partially activates the glycine site of the brain's NMDA receptor, studied as a fast-acting antidepressant.
PEPTIDES.evidence: A proof-of-concept trial suggested antidepressant effects104, but a phase 3 trial was terminated105 and it never reached approval.
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Long-term safety unknown; development stalled.105

PEPTIDES.name: Nemifitide
PEPTIDES.tag: An antidepressant peptide with mixed trial results.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic peptide studied as an injectable antidepressant.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mixed. In a placebo-controlled trial, it separated from placebo only in exploratory analyses of more severely depressed patients.106
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Side effects were similar to placebo in the trial.106

PEPTIDES.name: Neuropeptide Y
PEPTIDES.tag: A natural stress-buffering brain peptide. Early, small PTSD studies.
PEPTIDES.what: A natural brain peptide studied for stress-related disorders such as PTSD.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Early. In a dose-ranging study of 24 PTSD patients, single intranasal doses up to 9.6 mg were well tolerated and higher doses were linked to lower anxiety scores.107
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Only single-dose data in small studies.107

PEPTIDES.name: Cerebrolysin
PEPTIDES.tag: A brain-derived peptide mix used abroad for stroke and dementia. Cochrane finds weak evidence.
PEPTIDES.what: A mixture of peptides derived from animal brain tissue, given by injection or infusion.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Cochrane (2023): probably no benefit on death after acute stroke, with moderate-certainty evidence of a possible increase in non-fatal serious adverse events.108 For vascular dementia, evidence is weak and high risk of bias.109
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Possible increase in non-fatal serious adverse events (Cochrane).108
Animal-derived product; quality of imported versions is unverified.

PEPTIDES.name: Brimapitide
PEPTIDES.tag: A hearing-loss peptide that missed its phase 3 goal.
PEPTIDES.what: A peptide that targets the JNK stress-kinase pathway, tested for acute sudden hearing loss.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3 missed its primary endpoint; a post-hoc analysis suggested benefit in profound hearing loss.110
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Well tolerated in the trial; benefit unproven.110

PEPTIDES.name: Ziconotide
PEPTIDES.tag: A cone-snail-venom peptide approved for severe chronic pain, pumped directly into the spinal fluid.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic copy of a 25-amino-acid conopeptide from the marine snail Conus magus; it blocks N-type calcium channels in pain pathways.
PEPTIDES.evidence: FDA-approved for severe chronic pain when intrathecal therapy is warranted and other treatments fail or aren't tolerated.111
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved as Prialt (intrathecal infusion only).112,111
risks: Boxed warning: severe psychiatric symptoms and neurological impairment; contraindicated with a history of psychosis.111
Most common side effects: dizziness, nausea, confusion, abnormal eye movements (nystagmus).111

PEPTIDES.name: Pinealon
PEPTIDES.tag: A tripeptide 'bioregulator' from a Russian research group. Cell studies only.
PEPTIDES.what: A three-amino-acid peptide promoted as a brain 'bioregulator' by the Khavinson group in Russia.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Cell studies showed protection against oxidative stress.113 Human data are limited to a small uncontrolled Russian study (32 people), which also reported pro-oxidant activity and signs of suppressed blood-cell production.114
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No rigorous human safety data; one small study reported pro-oxidant effects and reduced blood stem-cell markers.114

PEPTIDES.name: ARA-290
PEPTIDES.tag: An EPO-derived peptide for nerve pain. Small, promising pilot trials only.
PEPTIDES.what: A non-erythropoietic peptide engineered from erythropoietin (EPO), meaning it is designed not to raise red blood cell counts.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Small pilot RCTs: improved small-fiber neuropathy symptoms in sarcoidosis115 and neuropathic symptoms and HbA1c in type 2 diabetes.116
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No safety concerns in small pilots, but larger trials are lacking.115,116

PEPTIDES.name: Dermorphin
PEPTIDES.tag: A potent opioid peptide from frog skin. Not a recovery aid; it's an opioid.
PEPTIDES.what: A seven-amino-acid (heptapeptide) opioid first isolated from the skin of an Amazonian frog in the early 1980s; in lab assays it was more potent than morphine.
PEPTIDES.evidence: A 1980s clinical study reported strong pain relief, but it was never followed up and the compound was never reintroduced clinically.117
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: It is a potent opioid; opioid-type risks apply.117
No modern human safety data.117

PEPTIDES.name: Thymosin Alpha-1
PEPTIDES.tag: An immune peptide with decades of trials. A big 2025 sepsis trial found no survival benefit.
PEPTIDES.what: An immune-modulating peptide (thymalfasin) studied for hepatitis and sepsis and sold online as an immune booster.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mixed. Hepatitis trials gave mixed results.118 The 2025 TESTS phase 3 trial in sepsis found no clear reduction in 28-day mortality.119
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. FDA's compounding safety page lists it among withdrawn nominations, noting inadequate safety information.33
risks: FDA says safety information is inadequate for compounding.33
Injection-site irritation was the main side effect in older trials.118

PEPTIDES.name: VIP
PEPTIDES.tag: A natural lung and gut peptide. Tested for COVID-19 lung failure without success.
PEPTIDES.what: A natural neuropeptide; aviptadil, its synthetic form, was tested as an IV treatment for COVID-19 respiratory failure.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Negative for COVID-19. The randomized, placebo-controlled TESICO trial found IV aviptadil did not improve recovery in COVID-19 respiratory failure.120
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. FDA declined requests for emergency use authorization of aviptadil for COVID-19.121
risks: Unproven for the uses marketed online.120

PEPTIDES.name: PNC-27
PEPTIDES.tag: Kills cancer cells in a dish. No human trials published.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic peptide that binds membrane-bound HDM-2 on cancer cells and disrupts their membranes and mitochondria in lab studies.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Cell-culture studies only.122 No published human trials found.
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No human safety or efficacy data.122

PEPTIDES.name: Cortistatin
PEPTIDES.tag: An anti-inflammatory neuropeptide in animal models. No human trials.
PEPTIDES.what: A natural neuropeptide studied as an anti-inflammatory target, mostly in animal models.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mostly animal and cell data, reviewed as a potential anti-inflammatory target.123
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No human safety data.123

PEPTIDES.name: Thymalin
PEPTIDES.tag: A Russian thymus-derived 'bioregulator'. Mostly cell studies.
PEPTIDES.what: A peptide preparation promoted in Russia for immune support.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mostly cell-model work from the Khavinson group.124
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No rigorous human safety data.124

PEPTIDES.name: Vilon
PEPTIDES.tag: A two-amino-acid 'bioregulator'. Mouse lifespan study only.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic dipeptide (lysine-glutamate) promoted as an immune and longevity bioregulator.
PEPTIDES.evidence: A 2000 mouse study reported fewer spontaneous tumors and longer life span.125 No controlled human trials found.
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No human safety data.125

PEPTIDES.name: IO102-IO103
PEPTIDES.tag: A peptide cancer vaccine for melanoma. Phase 3 narrowly missed its main goal.
PEPTIDES.what: An immune-modulating peptide vaccine given with the immunotherapy pembrolizumab in advanced melanoma.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3: adding the vaccine to pembrolizumab prolonged progression-free survival, but missed statistical significance on the primary endpoint.126
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Injection-site reactions in 56%; no added serious systemic toxicity in the trial.126

PEPTIDES.name: Pegcetacoplan
PEPTIDES.tag: An approved complement-blocking peptide for a rare blood disorder, kidney disease and eye disease.
PEPTIDES.what: Two identical 15-amino-acid peptides attached to a PEG chain; it is a complement inhibitor (blocks part of the immune system's complement cascade).
PEPTIDES.evidence: In PEGASUS, it beat eculizumab at improving hemoglobin in PNH.127
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved as Empaveli (PNH; C3 glomerulopathy / IC-MPGN)128 and Syfovre (geographic atrophy, by eye injection).129
risks: Boxed warning (Empaveli): serious infections from encapsulated bacteria such as meningococcus.128
Syfovre eye injections carry risks including endophthalmitis, retinal detachment and retinal vasculitis.129

PEPTIDES.name: Zilucoplan
PEPTIDES.tag: A daily self-injected peptide approved for myasthenia gravis.
PEPTIDES.what: A 15-amino-acid synthetic macrocyclic peptide that acts as a complement inhibitor.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3 RAISE showed rapid, clinically meaningful improvements in myasthenia gravis scores.130
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved for adults with anti-AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis.131
risks: Boxed warning: serious, potentially fatal meningococcal infections.131
Pancreatitis and pancreatic cysts reported; common effects include injection-site reactions, upper respiratory infection and diarrhea.131

PEPTIDES.name: Icotrokinra
PEPTIDES.tag: The first approved oral peptide pill that blocks the IL-23 receptor, for psoriasis.
PEPTIDES.what: A 13-amino-acid peptide taken by mouth that blocks the interleukin-23 receptor.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3 (ICONIC-LEAD): significantly more skin clearance at week 16 than placebo.132
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (March 2026)133 for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in adults and children 12+ weighing at least 40 kg.134
risks: Infection risk; screen for tuberculosis.134
Common: headache, nausea, cough, fungal infection, fatigue.134

PEPTIDES.name: Kisspeptin-10
PEPTIDES.tag: A natural hormone trigger that raises LH and testosterone in men. FDA keeps it on its safety list.
PEPTIDES.what: A short fragment of kisspeptin, a natural signal that switches on the reproductive hormone (LH/testosterone) cascade.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Human physiology studies: kisspeptin-10 strongly stimulates LH in men135, and 12 days of daily infusions sustained LH and testosterone rises.136 No trials of long-term use for 'testosterone boosting'.
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. On FDA's Category 2 list (503A), citing immunogenicity risk and little or no safety information.33 WADA bans kisspeptin and its analogues in male athletes.21
risks: FDA flags immunogenicity and limited safety data.33
Banned in sport (males).21

PEPTIDES.name: Gonadorelin
PEPTIDES.tag: Synthetic GnRH. Once FDA-approved, now discontinued; popular in TRT clinics.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic copy of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the brain signal that triggers LH and FSH release.
PEPTIDES.evidence: It has past FDA approvals (Factrel, Lutrepulse)137,138, but we found no controlled trials supporting its popular TRT-clinic use.
PEPTIDES.reg: Both FDA-approved products, Factrel and Lutrepulse, are listed as discontinued in Drugs@FDA.137,138 WADA bans GnRH and gonadorelin in male athletes.21
risks: No currently marketed FDA-approved product; compounded versions aren't FDA-reviewed.137,138
Banned in sport (males).21

PEPTIDES.name: Triptorelin
PEPTIDES.tag: An approved GnRH agonist for prostate cancer and early puberty. Sometimes misused to 'restart' hormones.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic 10-amino-acid GnRH agonist; with continued use it shuts down sex-hormone production.
PEPTIDES.evidence: FDA-approved for advanced prostate cancer (Trelstar)139 and central precocious puberty in children 2+ (Triptodur).140
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved.139,140 WADA bans GnRH agonist analogues including triptorelin in male athletes.21
risks: Early testosterone surge ('tumor flare') can worsen prostate cancer symptoms in the first weeks.139
Hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis; psychiatric events reported with GnRH agonists.139,140

PEPTIDES.name: Oxytocin
PEPTIDES.tag: The 'love hormone'. Approved for labor; nasal 'bonding' uses are unproven.
PEPTIDES.what: A nine-amino-acid (nonapeptide) pituitary hormone that triggers uterine contractions; Pitocin is made synthetically.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Approved for medically indicated labor induction and postpartum bleeding control.141
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved as an injection (Pitocin); the label says it is not indicated for elective induction of labor.141
risks: Reported maternal adverse reactions include uterine rupture, postpartum hemorrhage, cardiac arrhythmia and anaphylaxis.141

PEPTIDES.name: MVT-602
PEPTIDES.tag: A potent kisspeptin analogue studied to trigger ovulation in IVF.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic kisspeptin receptor agonist that triggers an LH surge.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Two small randomized trials in women: it produced an LH surge similar to the natural mid-cycle surge, with ovulation in 75–100% of women within 5 days depending on dose.142
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Small studies; long-term safety not established.142

PEPTIDES.name: Abaloparatide
PEPTIDES.tag: An approved bone-building injection for osteoporosis.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic 34-amino-acid analogue of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP 1-34) that stimulates new bone formation.
PEPTIDES.evidence: FDA-approved for postmenopausal women and men with osteoporosis at high fracture risk.143
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (Tymlos, 2017).144,143
risks: Avoid in people at increased risk of osteosarcoma (bone cancer).143
Common: high urine calcium, dizziness, nausea, headache, palpitations.143

PEPTIDES.name: Teriparatide
PEPTIDES.tag: The first approved bone-building peptide: the active piece of parathyroid hormone.
PEPTIDES.what: Identical to the first 34 amino acids (the active region) of human parathyroid hormone.
PEPTIDES.evidence: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis it reduces vertebral and nonvertebral fractures.145
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (Forteo).145
risks: Avoid in people at increased risk of osteosarcoma.145
Common: joint pain, pain, nausea.145

PEPTIDES.name: Linaclotide
PEPTIDES.tag: An approved 14-amino-acid peptide capsule for chronic constipation and IBS-C.
PEPTIDES.what: A 14-amino-acid peptide that activates guanylate cyclase-C in the gut, increasing fluid and speeding transit.
PEPTIDES.evidence: FDA-approved for IBS-C (adults and children 7+), chronic idiopathic constipation (adults) and functional constipation (children 2+).146
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (Linzess).146
risks: Boxed warning: contraindicated under age 2 (fatal dehydration in young mice).146
Diarrhea is the most common side effect and can be severe.146

PEPTIDES.name: Teduglutide
PEPTIDES.tag: An approved GLP-2 analogue that helps the gut absorb more in short bowel syndrome.
PEPTIDES.what: A 33-amino-acid analogue of GLP-2, a gut hormone that promotes growth of the intestinal lining.
PEPTIDES.evidence: FDA-approved for adults and children 1+ with short bowel syndrome who depend on IV (parenteral) nutrition.147
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (Gattex).147
risks: Warning: may accelerate growth of tumors; colonoscopy recommended after 1 year.147
Common: abdominal pain, nausea, bloating, injection-site reactions, fluid overload.147

PEPTIDES.name: Glepaglutide
PEPTIDES.tag: A long-acting GLP-2 analogue for short bowel syndrome. Mixed phase 3; not FDA-approved.
PEPTIDES.what: A long-acting GLP-2 analogue meant to reduce the need for IV nutrition in short bowel syndrome.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3: twice-weekly dosing reduced parenteral support, but once-weekly dosing was not statistically different from placebo.148
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Well tolerated in phase 3; once-weekly dose didn't work.148

PEPTIDES.name: Larazotide
PEPTIDES.tag: A 'leaky gut' tight-junction peptide for celiac disease. Phase 3 was stopped.
PEPTIDES.what: An oral peptide designed to tighten junctions between gut-lining cells, tested in celiac disease.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Mixed. In a randomized trial only the lowest dose (0.5 mg) beat placebo on symptoms149; a meta-analysis found benefit mainly during gluten challenge.150 The phase 3 trial was terminated.151
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Safety similar to placebo in trials; efficacy unproven.149

PEPTIDES.name: Epitalon
PEPTIDES.aka: Epithalon; N-acetyl epitalon amidate is a modified form
PEPTIDES.tag: The 'telomere peptide'. Cell and Russian animal studies; FDA has no safety data.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic pineal tetrapeptide (four amino acids) promoted as a 'bioregulator' that lengthens telomeres.
PEPTIDES.evidence: A 2003 cell study reported telomerase activation152; a 2025 review describes mostly cell, animal and Russian-group research.153 FDA says it has no safety information.33
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved. Removed from Category 2 in April 202617; an advisory committee voted in July 2026 to recommend it for the 503A list, but FDA hadn't acted as of Oct 9, 2026; a temporary enforcement-discretion stopgap was reported under consideration on Oct 7 (not announced or in effect).18,19,183 On Oct 14, 2026 FDA sent an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" to the White House regulatory office (OIRA) for review; it isn't published or in effect, and it doesn't name the peptides.187 OIRA has logged outside meetings on it for Oct 21, 23 and 27, and HHS Secretary Kennedy said on Oct 20 the goal is a regulated marketplace; the text still isn't public.189,190
risks: No safety information, per FDA.33

PEPTIDES.name: FOXO4-DRI
PEPTIDES.tag: A 'senolytic' peptide that cleared old cells in mice. No human data.
PEPTIDES.what: A designed peptide that disrupts FOXO4's interaction with p53, pushing senescent cells to self-destruct.
PEPTIDES.evidence: In a 2017 Cell paper, it restored fitness, fur density and kidney function in fast-aging and naturally aged mice.154
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No human safety data.154

PEPTIDES.name: Tat-Beclin-1
PEPTIDES.tag: A lab tool that switches on autophagy. Animal data only.
PEPTIDES.what: A cell-penetrating peptide built from part of the protein Beclin 1, designed to trigger autophagy (cellular clean-up).
PEPTIDES.evidence: A 2013 Nature study showed it induced autophagy, cut pathogen replication in cells, and reduced deaths in mice infected with chikungunya or West Nile virus.155
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No human safety data.155

PEPTIDES.name: Glutathione
PEPTIDES.tag: The body's master antioxidant tripeptide. Oral supplements raise levels; benefits are less clear.
PEPTIDES.what: A tripeptide made in the body that acts as a key antioxidant; sold as supplements and IV drips.
PEPTIDES.evidence: A 6-month RCT found daily oral glutathione raised body stores (e.g., +17–29% in blood at low dose) and lowered an oxidative stress marker.156 Hard clinical outcomes weren't studied.
PEPTIDES.reg: Sold as a dietary supplement; FDA does not approve supplements before sale.27
risks: Supplement quality varies; FDA doesn't review supplements for effectiveness before sale.27

Injectable compounded glutathione has quality risks too: on Oct 1, 2026 a 503A pharmacy recalled lots shipped nationwide (June 26–Sept 21, 2026) for possible elevated endotoxin, with two emergency-room reports.182

PEPTIDES.name: Carnosine
PEPTIDES.tag: A muscle dipeptide supplement. Modest blood-sugar effects in trials.
PEPTIDES.what: A dipeptide sold as an anti-aging, blood-sugar and performance supplement.
PEPTIDES.evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis of RCTs found carnosine or beta-alanine improved fasting glucose and HbA1c in prediabetes/type 2 diabetes, calling for more rigorous studies.157
PEPTIDES.reg: Sold as a dietary supplement; not FDA-approved.27
risks: Supplement quality is not FDA-verified before sale.27

PEPTIDES.name: Vesugen
PEPTIDES.tag: A Russian 'bioregulator' tripeptide for blood vessels. Small uncontrolled studies only.
PEPTIDES.what: A short synthetic tripeptide promoted by the Khavinson group as a blood-vessel bioregulator.
PEPTIDES.evidence: An uncontrolled study of 41 men with vascular erectile dysfunction reported improved penile blood flow158; a small uncontrolled study in older adults reported 'anti-aging' markers but also pro-oxidant activity.114
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: One study found pro-oxidant activity and signs of suppressed blood-cell production.114

PEPTIDES.name: Motixafortide
PEPTIDES.tag: An approved peptide that moves stem cells into the blood for collection in myeloma.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic cyclic peptide that blocks the CXCR4 receptor, which helps keep blood stem cells in the bone marrow.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3 GENESIS: with G-CSF, it mobilized far more stem cells within two collections than placebo plus G-CSF.159
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (2023)160 with filgrastim for stem-cell mobilization before autologous transplant in multiple myeloma.161
risks: Anaphylactic shock and hypersensitivity; premedication required.161
Common: injection-site reactions, itching, flushing, back pain.161

PEPTIDES.name: Rusfertide
PEPTIDES.tag: Newly approved (Aug 2026) hepcidin-mimicking peptide for polycythemia vera.
PEPTIDES.what: A synthetic cyclic peptide that mimics hepcidin, the body's iron-regulating hormone, to curb excess red blood cell production.
PEPTIDES.evidence: FDA-approved for erythrocytosis in adults with polycythemia vera.162
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved August 28, 2026 as Mimrylo.163
risks: New or worsening high platelet counts; monitor blood counts every 2–4 weeks at first.162
Injection-site reactions (56%) and anemia (16%) were most common.162

PEPTIDES.name: Enlicitide
PEPTIDES.tag: The first oral PCSK9-blocking pill: a macrocyclic peptide that lowers LDL cholesterol.
PEPTIDES.what: A macrocyclic peptide taken by mouth that binds PCSK9, leaving more LDL receptors to clear cholesterol.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Phase 3: LDL cholesterol fell 57.1% at 24 weeks vs a 3.0% rise on placebo.164
PEPTIDES.reg: FDA-approved (July 2026)165 as Lipfendra to lower LDL-C in adults with hypercholesterolemia, including HeFH.166
risks: Most common side effects: diarrhea and dizziness.166

PEPTIDES.name: Risuteganib
PEPTIDES.tag: An integrin-blocking eye peptide for dry AMD. Early, inconclusive trials.
PEPTIDES.what: An integrin inhibitor peptide studied for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and diabetic macular edema.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Early phase 1/2 trials; a 2020 review says more data are needed before it can be evaluated for clinical use.167
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: Benefit unproven; more data needed.167

PEPTIDES.name: Prostamax
PEPTIDES.tag: A Russian prostate 'bioregulator'. Rat tissue-culture data only.
PEPTIDES.what: A short synthetic peptide promoted as a prostate bioregulator.
PEPTIDES.evidence: Only rat tissue-culture work was found.168
PEPTIDES.reg: Not FDA-approved.
risks: No human safety data.168

semaglutide.short: Label: 0.25 mg weekly → titrate to 1.7–2.4 mg (Wegovy)
semaglutide.html: Wegovy (chronic weight management): start 0.25 mg by subcutaneous injection once weekly for 4 weeks, then step up every 4 weeks to 0.5 mg, 1 mg and 1.7 mg; adult maintenance is 2.4 mg (recommended) or 1.7 mg once weekly; 2.4 mg for ages 12+.169 Ozempic (type 2 diabetes): 0.25 mg weekly for 4 weeks, then 0.5 mg weekly; may increase to 1 mg, then 2 mg, each after at least 4 weeks.170

tirzepatide.html: Zepbound (weight reduction, obstructive sleep apnea): start 2.5 mg subcutaneously once weekly for 4 weeks (a starting dose only, not a maintenance dose), then increase in 2.5 mg steps after at least 4 weeks; maintenance 5, 10 or 15 mg weekly for weight (10 or 15 mg for sleep apnea); maximum 15 mg weekly.171 Mounjaro (type 2 diabetes): same start and steps; maximum 15 mg weekly in adults, 10 mg in children 10+.172

retatrutide.html: Phase 2 (48 weeks): 1, 4, 8 or 12 mg by subcutaneous injection once weekly, some arms starting at 2 mg; side effects were partly reduced with a lower starting dose.173

bpc157.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA says it has identified no or only limited safety information for proposed routes and lacks enough information to know whether it would cause harm in humans.33

tb500.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA says it has not identified any human exposure data for TB-500.33

ghkcu.html: GHK-Cu is sold in cosmetic serums, but there is no established or tested dose for injected use. For injectable GHK-Cu, FDA notes immunogenicity concerns and limited human safety data.33 A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose.

cjcipa.short: No established dose; FDA safety flags
cjcipa.html: No established or approved dose for the combination; a community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only. For reference only, small studies used: CJC-1295 single or repeated subcutaneous doses, best tolerated at 30 or 60 µg/kg, in healthy adults174; ipamorelin 0.03 mg/kg IV twice daily for up to 7 days after bowel surgery.175 FDA cites serious adverse events with CJC-1295 (increased heart rate, vasodilatory reaction) and serious adverse events including death with IV ipamorelin.33

collagen.html: Oral collagen products have been tested at various daily amounts; the meta-analyses cited here don't support a single standard dose.25,26

ss31.html: Forzinity (Barth syndrome): 40 mg subcutaneously once daily for patients weighing at least 30 kg; 20 mg once daily in adults with eGFR under 30 mL/min not on dialysis.176

pt141.short: Label: 1.75 mg as needed; max 1/24 h
pt141.html: Vyleesi (HSDD in premenopausal women): 1.75 mg subcutaneously by autoinjector, as needed, at least 45 minutes before anticipated sexual activity; no more than one dose in 24 hours, and more than 8 doses a month is not recommended.29

liraglutide.html: Saxenda (weight management): start 0.6 mg subcutaneously once daily for one week, then increase weekly until 3 mg daily.38 Victoza (type 2 diabetes): 0.6 mg daily for one week, then 1.2 mg daily; may increase to 1.8 mg daily.177

exenatide.html: Byetta (type 2 diabetes): 5 mcg subcutaneously twice daily within 60 minutes before the morning and evening meals; may increase to 10 mcg twice daily after 1 month. Do not give after a meal.40

pramlintide.html: Symlin (diabetes on mealtime insulin): cut mealtime insulin by 50% when starting. Type 1: 15 mcg subcutaneously before major meals, raised in 15 mcg steps to 30 or 60 mcg. Type 2: 60 mcg before major meals, then 120 mcg as tolerated. Wait at least 3 days between changes.43 Note: Drugs@FDA lists Symlin as discontinued.44

setmelanotide.short: Label: start 0.5–2 mg daily → 3 mg daily
setmelanotide.html: Imcivree (approved rare obesity indications): starting dose depends on indication and age, e.g., 2 mg subcutaneously once daily for 2 weeks (age 12+ with BBS or POMC/PCSK1/LEPR deficiency) or 0.5 mg daily for 2 weeks (acquired hypothalamic obesity, age 4+); recommended maintenance for ages 6+ is 3 mg once daily.46

survodutide.short: Trial doses: up to 3.6 or 6.0 mg weekly
survodutide.html: SYNCHRONIZE-1: subcutaneous injection once weekly, adjusted up to 3.6 mg or 6.0 mg, for 76 weeks.48

mazdutide.html: GLORY-1: 4 mg or 6 mg once weekly for 48 weeks.49

cagrilintide.html: Phase 2: 0.3, 0.6, 1.2, 2.4 or 4.5 mg subcutaneously once weekly for 26 weeks.50

cagrisema.html: REDEFINE 1: cagrilintide 2.4 mg plus semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly for 68 weeks.51

amycretin.short: Trial doses: up to 60 mg weekly
amycretin.html: Phase 1b/2a: once-weekly subcutaneous doses escalated up to 60 mg (36 weeks), or to maintenance doses of 20 mg, 5 mg or 1.25 mg.52

eloralintide.html: Phase 2: 1, 3, 6 or 9 mg subcutaneously once weekly, or escalations of 3→9 mg and 6→9 mg, for 48 weeks.53

petrelintide.html: Phase 1: 0.6 or 1.2 mg once weekly for 6 doses, or 16 weekly doses escalated every 2 weeks to 2.4, 4.8 or 9.0 mg.55

pemvidutide.html: 1.2, 1.8 or 2.4 mg subcutaneously once weekly for 12 weeks.57

cotadutide.html: Phase 2b: 100, 200 or 300 µg by subcutaneous injection, with HbA1c and weight assessed to 54 weeks.58

ecnoglutide.html: Phase 3: 1.2, 1.8 or 2.4 mg subcutaneously once weekly for 40 weeks.59

vk2735.html: VENTURE: once-weekly subcutaneous doses from 2.5 mg to 15 mg for 13 weeks.60

ct388.html: Phase 1: single doses of 0.5–7.5 mg, or 4 once-weekly doses of 5–12 mg, subcutaneously.62

taspoglutide.html: T-emerge 2: 10 mg or 20 mg subcutaneously once weekly.64

berobenatide.short: Trial doses: weekly; mg not disclosed
berobenatide.html: Phase 2b VESPER-1: four dose levels given subcutaneously once weekly without titration65; phase 3 uses three subcutaneous dose arms.66 The registry entries don't state the mg amounts.

gubamy.html: Phase 1: single, then multiple, subcutaneous doses (5 mg/mL solution)67; phase 2 escalates six arms to maintenance doses.68 The registry entries don't state the mg amounts.

ribupatide.short: Trial doses: up to 5.4 mg weekly ×4
ribupatide.html: First-in-human: single doses of 0.1–8.1 mg, and 4 once-weekly subcutaneous doses up to 5.4 mg.69

zovaglutide.html: Phase 2 (company-reported): 80 mg or 160 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks or every 2 weeks, for 24 weeks71; phase 3 doses are given every 4 weeks.72

aod9604.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA reports little or no safety information and serious adverse events that may be associated.33

motsc.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA says it has no human exposure data.33

adipotide.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. Data are from monkeys only.76

kpv.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA says it has no human exposure data.33

ll37.html: Topical on venous leg ulcers: 0.5, 1.6 or 3.2 mg/mL (lower two showed benefit in the 2014 trial).78 No injected dose has been tested in trials.

mgf.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA says it has no human exposure data for PEG-MGF.33

tesamorelin.html: Egrifta WR (HIV-associated abdominal fat): 1.28 mg subcutaneously once daily into the abdomen. Egrifta SV is a different formulation with different dosing; the two are not interchangeable.83

sermorelin.html: No current FDA label is available because Geref is discontinued.85 For reference only: a 1999 review describes the regimen studied in children with growth hormone deficiency, 30 µg/kg subcutaneously once daily, and a single 1 µg/kg IV dose as a diagnostic test.84 These are not adult or 'anti-aging' doses.

hexarelin.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. Reviews describe few rigorous studies and unknown long-term safety.86

ghrp6.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA keeps it on its Category 2 list, citing immunogenicity, cortisol effects and higher blood glucose.33

afamelanotide.html: Scenesse (EPP): one 16 mg implant inserted under the skin above the hip bone every 2 months by a trained health professional.89

melanotan2.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA cites case reports of melanoma, PRES, sympathomimetic toxidrome and priapism.33

argireline.html: In the 21-person crow's-feet trial, the cream was applied twice daily around the eyes; the abstract doesn't state the concentration.93

matrixyl.html: In the 21-person crow's-feet trial, the cream was applied twice daily around the eyes; the abstract doesn't state the concentration.93

os01.html: Tested as a topical skincare formulation; the published abstract doesn't state a concentration.96

semax.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA says it has no or limited safety information.33 Small Russian studies exist, but their abstracts don't give doses we could verify.97

selank.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA says it lacks important safety information.33

dihexa.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. FDA says it has no human exposure data by any route.33

dsip.html: No established or approved dose. For reference only: the 1992 insomnia study gave 25 nmol/kg IV on three afternoons and found no major benefit.100 FDA says it has no safety information for the proposed route.33

pe2228.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. Data are from mice only.101

humanin.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. We don't list community, vendor or 'protocol' amounts. Research is cell and animal only.102

davunetide.short: Trial doses: 30 mg nasal twice daily
davunetide.html: Phase 2/3 in PSP: 30 mg intranasally twice daily for 52 weeks (not effective).103

rapastinel.html: Proof-of-concept: a single IV dose of 1, 5, 10 or 30 mg/kg; 5 and 10 mg/kg reduced symptoms for about a week.104

nemifitide.html: 30 mg/day or 45 mg/day by subcutaneous injection, 5 days a week for 2 weeks.106

npy.html: Single intranasal doses of 1.4 to 9.6 mg in a dose-ranging PTSD study.107

cerebrolysin.short: Trial regimen: e.g., 30 mL daily ×10 days
cerebrolysin.html: Stroke trials used daily regimens such as 30 mL a day for 10 days; a Cochrane review found the increase in non-fatal serious adverse events more prominent with that 30 mL × 10-day schedule.108

brimapitide.short: Trial doses: single 0.4–0.8 mg/mL ear injection
brimapitide.html: Phase 3: a single intratympanic (through the eardrum) injection of 0.4 or 0.8 mg/mL.110

ziconotide.html: Prialt (severe chronic pain): intrathecal infusion only (not IV), by a physician experienced with implanted pumps. Start at no more than 2.4 mcg/day and increase by up to 2.4 mcg/day no more than 2–3 times a week, to a recommended maximum of 19.2 mcg/day by day 21.111

pinealon.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. The small Russian human study abstract doesn't give a dose.114

ara290.html: Pilot trials: 2 mg IV three times weekly (sarcoidosis)115; 4 mg subcutaneously daily for 28 days (type 2 diabetes).116

dermorphin.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. We don't list community, vendor or 'protocol' amounts. It is a potent opioid; the 1980s clinical study was never followed up.117

thymosina1.html: Hepatitis trials: 1.6 mg subcutaneously twice a week.118 TESTS sepsis trial: subcutaneous injection every 12 hours for 7 days (no mortality benefit).119

vip.html: TESICO (COVID-19): aviptadil as a 12-hour IV infusion daily for 3 days, targeting 600, 1,200 and 1,800 pmol/kg (no benefit).120

pnc27.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. We don't list community, vendor or 'protocol' amounts. Data are from cell studies only.122

cortistatin.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. We don't list community, vendor or 'protocol' amounts. Data are mostly animal and cell studies.123

thymalin.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. Data are mostly cell studies.124

vilon.html: No established or tested human dose exists; FDA has not approved it for any use. A community protocol from researchcfps.com is shown below for education only; it is not a tested or approved dose. Data are from mice.125

io102.html: Phase 3: IO102-IO103 85 µg each subcutaneously, with pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks, for up to 2 years.126

pegcetacoplan.html: Empaveli (PNH; C3G/IC-MPGN): 1,080 mg subcutaneously twice weekly in adults (weight-based in children with C3G/IC-MPGN); vaccinate against encapsulated bacteria at least 2 weeks before starting.128 Syfovre (geographic atrophy): 15 mg intravitreal injection into each affected eye every 25 to 60 days, by a physician.129

zilucoplan.html: Zilbrysq (AChR+ generalized myasthenia gravis): once-daily subcutaneous dose by body weight: 16.6 mg (under 56 kg), 23 mg (56 to under 77 kg), 32.4 mg (77 kg and up). Meningococcal vaccination at least 2 weeks before starting.131

icotrokinra.html: Icotyde (plaque psoriasis): 200 mg by mouth once daily on waking, on an empty stomach with water; wait at least 30 minutes before eating.134
